title: Diplopia in a patient presenting with “blurred vision”: a case report
case_prompt:
A 50-year-old African-American woman with hypertension presented with a two-week history of blurred vision associated with facial discomfort and a generalized headache. She denied fever, speech or swallowing problems, weakness, numbness, gait disturbance, preceding infection, or recent vaccination.

On examination, there was swelling of the left upper eyelid. Extraocular movements revealed that the right eye failed to move in the horizontal plane, and the left eye had impaired adduction with normal abduction, consistent with a pseudo 1 and ½ syndrome. The left upper eyelid was ptotic, and on upgaze the left eye failed to elevate fully. A Cogan lid twitch was positive. Visual acuity, fundoscopic examination, and the remainder of her neurologic examination were normal. The patient declined the ice pack test.

Investigations to rule out central etiologies—including CT of the orbits, MRI of the brain, MRA, MRV, and routine blood tests—were unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Central brainstem 1 and ½ syndrome was considered but excluded because “Investigative studies to rule out emergent central etiologies with computed tomography (CT) orbits, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) of the brain, along with blood work, were unremarkable.”  
2. Orbital cellulitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis were considered given eyelid swelling and headache but were excluded as “orbital cellulitis, and cavernous sinus thrombosis had also to be ruled out.”  
3. Miller–Fisher syndrome was considered in the differential of a pseudo 1 and ½ syndrome—“When considering a pseudo 1 and ½ syndrome, the Miller–Fisher variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome … must be considered”—but lack of areflexia/ataxia and negative anti-GQ1b made it unlikely: “Antibodies against GQ1b are present in most patients with MFS.”  
4. Graves’ ophthalmopathy may cause diplopia and eyelid changes but was excluded because “it can be differentiated from MG by the lack of ptosis. Other features found in Graves’ disease such as proptosis, lid retraction, lid lag, and periorbital edema are not seen with OMG.”  
5. Mitochondrial ophthalmoplegias were considered—“chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia and Kearns–Sayre syndrome, both of which are mitochondrial disorders”—but their slow, progressive course did not match this acute presentation.  
6. Structural lesions such as aneurysms or parasellar tumors were ruled out by normal imaging: “structural diseases of the brainstem such as aneurysms and parasellar tumors.”
